s0698: Planes don’t flap their wings like birds. The wings stay still while the engines push the plane forward, so air rushes over the wings and lifts it up.
s0701: After check-in, your suitcase rides on long conveyor belts under the airport, past scanners, all the way to your plane.
s0703: Big planes fly higher than most clouds. That’s why it can be sunny outside your window even when it’s raining on the ground.
s0705: Your ears pop when the plane climbs or comes down because the air pressure changes. Swallowing or yawning helps them feel better.
s0707: Big passenger jets always have at least two pilots: the captain and the first officer. They share the flying.
s0710: On a night flight you may spot the lights of whole cities from your window, glittering like maps.
s0712: Dry cabin air and lower pressure dull your sense of taste for salty and sweet by about a third, so airline chefs add extra flavour.
s0714: Airliner tyres are filled with nitrogen, not ordinary air, because nitrogen stays steady when it gets very cold or very hot.
s0716: Every plane has a red light on its left wingtip and a green light on its right, so pilots can tell which way another plane is heading.
s0718: Air traffic controllers in the control tower tell every plane when it may take off and land, like referees for the sky.
s0720: Hong Kong International Airport sits on a huge platform made by flattening the islands of Chek Lap Kok and Lam Chau and filling in the sea around them.
s0723: Geese fly in a V so each bird rides on the swirling air from the one in front, which saves energy on long journeys.
s0725: Runway numbers are compass directions with the last zero dropped. Runway 25 points about 250°, roughly west-south-west.
s0727: Much of a jet’s fuel is stored inside its wings. A long-haul A350 can carry well over 100,000 litres.
s0729: Jet streams are fast rivers of wind high in the sky. Flying east with one can make a long trip an hour or more shorter.
s0731: The wheels fold into the plane after take-off. Tucked away, they don’t catch the air, so the plane flies more smoothly and uses less fuel.
s0733: Pilots spell words with the phonetic alphabet — Alfa, Bravo, Charlie… — so letters like B and D never get mixed up on the radio.
s0735: The white lines behind planes are contrails: water vapour from the engines that freezes into tiny ice crystals in the cold air.
s0738: Flight recorders, nicknamed black boxes, are actually painted bright orange so they are easy to find.
s0740: At cruising height the air outside is often colder than −50 °C, while the cabin is kept comfortable at around 22 °C.
s0742: Flying west, you travel with the Sun. A 14-hour flight from Hong Kong to London may land only 6 or 7 clock-hours after it left.
s0744: The shortest route between two places on a globe is a curve called a great circle. That’s why flights to North America often head up towards the Arctic.
s0746: The cabin is pressurised to feel like being on a mountain about 1,800 to 2,400 metres high, not at sea level.
s0747: A plane made of carbon fibre
s0748: More than half of an A350’s structure is carbon-fibre composite, which is lighter than aluminium and doesn’t rust.
s0750: Wings make lift by turning air downward. Their curved shape and slight tilt (the angle of attack) create lower pressure above the wing than below it.
s0752: Mach 1 is the speed of sound. Airliners cruise around Mach 0.85 — in the thin, cold air up high, that’s about 900 km/h.
s0754: Planes find their position using GPS satellites plus inertial systems: gyroscopes and accelerometers that track every movement without any outside signal.
s0756: The nose cone hides a weather radar that spots storms hundreds of kilometres ahead, so pilots can steer around them.
s0758: In steady flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Change one and the plane climbs, descends, speeds up or slows down.
s0760: Sustainable aviation fuel can be made from used cooking oil and waste. Over its life it can cut carbon emissions by up to about 80% compared with fossil jet fuel.
s0762: A fully loaded A350 weighs about as much as 50 elephants — and it still flies!
s0764: Each main door on a big plane hides an inflatable slide, ready in case everyone needs to get off quickly.
s0766: Plane kitchens are called galleys. Meals are cooked on the ground, then heated in special ovens on board.
s0768: Planes can’t reverse by themselves at the gate, so a small, strong truck called a tug pushes them back.
s0770: From a plane you can sometimes see a rainbow as a full circle, because there’s no ground to cut it in half.
s0772: The tiny hole in your window is a breather hole. It balances the air pressure between the window panes.
s0774: Wings bend upward a little in flight, like a diving board. They are built to flex, which makes them strong.
s0776: Flying east overnight, you race towards the morning, so the sunrise can come only a few hours after sunset.
s0778: Flying fish can glide above the waves for more than 50 metres, using their big fins like wings.
s0780: Eagles glide for ages without flapping by riding rising warm air called thermals. Glider pilots do the same!
s0783: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
s0785: When the seatbelt sign is on, stay buckled. It keeps you safe if the plane flies through bumpy air.
s0787: Turbulence is just bumpy air, a bit like waves on the sea. Planes are built to handle it easily.
s0789: Hong Kong’s airport is so big that an automatic train carries passengers between the gates.
s0791: The two pilots usually eat different meals, so if one meal made someone unwell, the other pilot would be fine.
s0793: Specially trained dogs help at airports by sniffing out things that aren’t allowed, like some fresh foods.
s0795: Clouds are made of tiny water drops or ice crystals so light that they float in the air.
s0797: About 71% of Earth’s surface is ocean, so on long flights you often fly over lots of sea.
s0799: Penguins can’t fly in the air, but they “fly” underwater, using their wings as flippers.
s0801: A honeybee beats its wings about 200 times every second — that’s what makes the buzz.
s0803: Space begins about 100 km up. Airliners fly at about 11 km, so space is around nine times higher.
s0805: Babies often cry at take-off and landing because of ear pressure. Drinking milk helps them swallow and feel better.
s0807: Seat letters go across the plane. On many planes, A is a window seat on the left side.
s0809: The barcode on your boarding pass holds your name, flight and seat — that’s how Sky Cadets knows your flight!
s0811: On a clear night flight, far from city lights, you can sometimes see more stars than from the ground.
s0813: The Pacific is the biggest ocean on Earth — bigger than all the land put together.
s0815: Mount Everest is 8,849 metres tall. Airliners usually fly even higher, at about 10,000 to 12,000 metres.
s0817: A blue whale can grow to about 30 metres long — almost half the length of an A350.
s0819: An A350 stands about 17 metres tall at its tail — as high as three giraffes standing on top of each other.
s0821: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth.
s0823: For short journeys, trains usually make much less pollution per passenger than planes.
s0825: Trees soak up carbon dioxide from the air, which is why planting forests helps our planet.
s0827: There are seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
s0829: Kites were invented in China more than 2,000 years ago — some of the first things people made to fly.
s0831: Planes take off and land facing into the wind. It gives extra lift, so they need less runway.
s0833: Lights along the cabin floor show the way to the exits if it ever gets dark or smoky.
s0835: The life vest near your seat has a whistle and a little light, so rescuers can find you.
s0837: Many countries don’t allow fresh fruit in your bag, to stop pests and plant diseases spreading.
s0839: Before take-off the cabin crew check every door is closed and its slide is ready.
s0841: Painting a big jet can take more than a week and uses hundreds of litres of paint.
s0843: In 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight. It lasted 12 seconds and went 37 metres — shorter than an A350’s wingspan.
s0845: Cabin crew train for weeks in safety, first aid and firefighting. Serving meals is only one part of the job.
s0847: The bent-up tips on many wings, called winglets or sharklets, calm the swirling air at the tip and save fuel.
s0849: Most planes are mostly white because white reflects sunlight, keeping the plane cooler, and makes damage easier to spot.
s0851: Cabin lights are dimmed for night take-offs and landings so your eyes are ready for the dark if you ever need to get out.
s0853: Window blinds stay open for take-off and landing so the crew can see outside and your eyes adjust to the light.
s0855: Every airline has a two-letter code. Cathay Pacific’s is CX — that’s why your flight number starts with CX.
s0857: Airports have three-letter codes: HKG is Hong Kong, LHR is London Heathrow and NRT is Tokyo Narita.
s0859: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
s0861: Common swifts can stay in the air for ten months without landing — they even sleep while flying.
s0863: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird — up to about 3.5 metres.
s0865: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, not just glide.
s0867: Cumulonimbus storm clouds can tower more than 12 km high — higher than planes fly — so pilots go around them.
s0869: Planes are built to handle lightning. The electricity runs along the skin and out again, keeping everyone inside safe.
s0871: Fog is a cloud touching the ground. Special landing systems help pilots land even when they can’t see far.
s0873: Hong Kong warns of typhoons with signals numbered 1, 3, 8, 9 and 10. Signal 10 is the strongest.
s0875: Hong Kong International Airport is one of the world’s busiest cargo airports, moving millions of tonnes of goods every year.
s0877: London Heathrow is one of the busiest airports in Europe, with well over 70 million passengers a year.
s0879: Plane toilets use a powerful vacuum instead of lots of water, which saves weight.
s0881: Big jets carry hundreds of litres of fresh water for drinks, tea, coffee and washing hands.
s0883: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth. Singapore is less than 150 km north of it.
s0885: When it’s summer in Hong Kong, it’s winter in Sydney, because they are on opposite sides of the equator.
s0887: Fly across the International Date Line in the Pacific and the date jumps by a whole day!
s0889: The Airbus A380 is the world’s largest passenger plane, with two full decks from front to back.
s0891: Concorde flew passengers faster than the speed of sound, crossing from London to New York in about three and a half hours.
s0893: Pilots and controllers around the world use English as the common language of the radio, so everyone understands each other.
s0895: Between flights, ground crew unload bags, refuel, clean the cabin and check the tyres — often in about an hour.
s0897: Before an engine is approved, engineers fire bird-sized objects into it to prove it can cope.
s0899: A big jet engine’s fan is about 3 metres across — wide enough for a grown-up to stand inside.
s0901: On a long flight the fuel can weigh more than all the passengers and their bags together.
s0903: Cabin air is drier than most deserts, so it’s a good idea to drink water on long flights.
s0905: Cabin air is refreshed every few minutes, and filters catch tiny particles, including germs.
s0907: The longest mountain range on Earth is under the ocean: the Mid-Ocean Ridge, about 65,000 km long.
s0909: Flights from Hong Kong to Europe can pass over the Gobi Desert, a huge cold desert in Mongolia and China.
s0911: A red kangaroo can hop at more than 50 km/h and cover about 8 metres in a single leap.
s0913: Giant pandas can spend up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.
s0915: London’s red double-decker buses have carried passengers for more than 100 years.
s0917: Aircraft engineers inspect planes on a strict schedule, from quick walk-around checks to huge overhauls that take weeks.
s0919: X-ray machines let security officers see inside bags without opening them, keeping dangerous items off planes.
s0921: Cabin crew on international flights often speak several languages so they can help passengers from around the world.
s0923: Pilots use the autopilot for much of a long flight, but they are always watching, checking and ready to fly by hand.
s0925: Before take-off and landing, panels slide out of the wings, called flaps and slats. They make the wing bigger and curvier for flying slowly.
s0927: After landing, panels pop up on top of the wings. These spoilers “spoil” the lift so the wheels press down and the brakes work better.
s0929: That roar after touchdown is reverse thrust: the engines redirect air forward to help slow the plane.
s0931: Each plane is given a four-digit transponder code so controllers can identify it on their radar screens.
s0933: When an airport is busy, planes may fly racetrack-shaped loops called holding patterns while they wait their turn to land.
s0935: Pilots call altitude “flight levels”: Flight Level 380 means about 38,000 feet.
s0937: Pilots measure speed in knots. One knot is one nautical mile per hour, about 1.85 km/h.
s0939: A nautical mile is based on Earth’s size: one-sixtieth of a degree of latitude, about 1,852 metres.
s0941: An airliner touches down at about 250 km/h, so its tyres spin up from zero in a split second — that’s the puff of smoke you sometimes see.
s0943: Airliner brakes are often made of carbon and can get hotter than 500 °C after a heavy landing.
s0945: The Instrument Landing System sends radio beams along the runway so a plane can follow an invisible slope down to the ground.
s0947: When Hong Kong’s new airport opened in 1998, it replaced Kai Tak, famous for its tricky landings between tall buildings.
s0949: Hong Kong’s airport opened its third runway in 2022, part of its Three-Runway System.
s0951: Earth spins at about 1,670 km/h at the equator — faster than a jet flies — but we don’t feel it because everything moves with us.
s0953: Planes cruise high because the air is thin, so there is less drag and the engines burn less fuel.
s0955: At cruising height the air pressure outside is only about a quarter of sea level — far too thin to breathe without pressurisation.
s0956: Over the top of the world
s0957: Some flights between Asia and North America fly over the Arctic, because the great-circle route that way is shorter.
s0959: Hong Kong to London usually takes longer than London to Hong Kong, because high-altitude winds mostly blow from west to east.
s0961: If cabin pressure dropped, oxygen masks would fall from above. Put yours on first, then help others.
s0963: Many cabin oxygen masks are fed by chemical generators that make oxygen for around 12 to 20 minutes, while the pilots descend to thicker air.
s0965: Big planes leave spinning air behind them, so controllers keep the next plane a safe distance back.
s0967: Pilots of big jets add “Heavy” to their call sign on the radio, like “Cathay 251 Heavy”, to warn others about their strong wake.
s0969: When something flies faster than sound, it makes a sonic boom — a loud bang like thunder.
s0971: Cirrus clouds are made of ice and float very high. Their name comes from the Latin word for a curl of hair.
s0973: You see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and rain is in front of you.
s0975: A monsoon is a seasonal change of wind that brings heavy summer rain to much of South and South-East Asia.
s0977: Glaciers and ice sheets hold about two-thirds of all the fresh water on Earth.
s0979: The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimetres a year, as India slowly pushes into the rest of Asia.
s0981: The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 cm taller in summer, because iron expands when it’s warm.
s0983: Greater Tokyo is the world’s most populous city area, home to more than 37 million people.
s0985: The roof of the Sydney Opera House is covered in more than one million tiles.
s0987: Bangkok’s full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world — about 168 letters in English.
s0989: Vancouver sits between sea and mountains: on some days you can ski in the morning and walk on the beach in the afternoon.
s0991: New York’s subway has more than 470 stations — more than any other metro in the world.
s0993: Singapore’s Changi Airport has the Rain Vortex, an indoor waterfall about 40 metres tall.
s0995: In 1783 a Montgolfier hot-air balloon carried the first people into the sky, over Paris.
s0997: In 1932 Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.
s0999: Cathay Pacific was founded in Hong Kong in 1946 by an American pilot and an Australian pilot.
s1001: Small electric planes already fly today, and engineers are working on bigger ones for short trips.
s1003: Before take-off, pilots calculate key speeds: V1 (the decision speed), VR (when to lift the nose) and V2 (a safe climbing speed).
s1005: Before every flight, the crew work out the exact weight of fuel, passengers, bags and cargo. It changes the take-off speed and the runway needed.
s1007: Bags and cargo are loaded so the plane’s centre of gravity stays in a safe range — too far forward or back makes it harder to control.
s1009: Some long-haul jets can dump fuel in an emergency to get down to a safe landing weight quickly.
s1011: Twin-engine jets flying far over oceans follow ETOPS rules, which limit how far they may be from an airport where they could land.
s1012: A tiny engine in the tail
s1013: A small jet engine in the tail, the APU, powers the lights and air conditioning while the main engines are off.
s1015: If all power were lost, a small propeller called a ram air turbine swings out and spins in the wind to make emergency electricity.
s1017: In fly-by-wire planes like the A350, the pilots’ controls send electrical signals to computers, which move the control surfaces.
s1019: Airbus pilots steer with a small sidestick, a bit like a games joystick, instead of a big control wheel.
s1021: Important systems on a plane have backups, so if one part stops working, another takes over.
s1023: Modern jet engines push most of their air around the hot core rather than through it. This bypass air makes them quieter and more efficient.
s1025: Inside a jet engine, gas can reach over 1,500 °C — hotter than the blades’ melting point — so the blades are cooled by air flowing through tiny holes.
s1027: As a plane burns fuel and gets lighter, it can climb higher where the air is thinner and flying is more efficient. This is called a step climb.
s1029: Because Earth spins, moving air curves — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. This Coriolis effect is why typhoons rotate.
s1031: The eye of a typhoon can be calm, even with blue sky, while the strongest winds swirl in the eyewall around it.
s1033: Clear-air turbulence happens in cloudless skies, often near jet streams, so pilots share reports to warn each other.
s1035: Ice on wings spoils lift, so planes have anti-ice systems, and on cold days they are sprayed with de-icing fluid before take-off.
s1037: Airliners cruise near the top of the troposphere, the layer of air where almost all weather happens. Above it lies the calmer stratosphere.
s1039: The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet rays.
s1041: Hot air is thinner, so on hot days planes need more runway to take off.
s1043: At very high airports like El Alto in Bolivia, the air is so thin that planes need extra-long runways.
s1045: Earth’s magnetic north pole drifts every year, so runway numbers sometimes have to be changed!
s1047: Every place has an address of latitude and longitude. Hong Kong’s airport is at about 22° N, 114° E.
s1049: The Prime Meridian, 0° longitude, runs through Greenwich in London — the starting point for the world’s time zones.
s1051: Pilots use one world time, UTC (“Zulu”), for flight plans and reports, so nobody gets confused by time zones.
s1053: Jet lag happens because your body clock is still on home time. Getting daylight at your destination helps reset it.
s1055: At Kai Tak, pilots aimed at a red-and-white checkerboard on a hill, then made a sharp turn to line up with the runway.
s1057: The world’s first jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, began carrying passengers in 1952.
s1059: The Boeing 747 “Jumbo Jet”, first flown in 1969, carried far more passengers than earlier airliners and made long trips more affordable.
s1061: One flight recorder keeps cockpit sounds; the other stores thousands of flight measurements. Together they help make flying ever safer.
s1063: Flying with a major airline is one of the safest ways to travel, partly because every incident is studied and the lessons are shared worldwide.
s1065: Air traffic control is split up: the tower looks after the runway, approach control the nearby skies, and area centres the high cruising flights.
s1067: Hong Kong is a hub: many passengers change planes here on their way between other cities.
s1069: Long-lasting contrails can trap heat, especially at night, so researchers are testing flight paths that avoid making them.
s1071: A full plane uses fuel more efficiently than an empty one, because the fuel is shared among more people.
s1073: Every kilogram saved on a plane saves fuel on every flight, so airlines use lighter seats, trolleys and materials.
s1075: Engineers are studying hydrogen-powered planes, which would give off water vapour instead of carbon dioxide.
s1077: Many airports now use solar panels and electric ground vehicles to cut pollution.
s1079: Despite the myth, the Great Wall of China is very hard to see from space with the naked eye — it is long but narrow.
s1081: When a plane retires, most of it — often well over three-quarters by weight — can be reused or recycled.
s1083: In aviation a stall has nothing to do with engines: it means the wing’s angle to the air is too steep, the airflow breaks away from the top, and lift collapses.
s1084: Lift and the square of speed
s1085: Lift grows with the square of speed: fly twice as fast and, with everything else the same, a wing makes four times the lift.
s1087: Swirling wingtip vortices cause induced drag. Long, slender wings reduce it — which is why gliders and the A350 have such long wings.
s1089: Airliner wings are supercritical: fairly flat on top to delay the shock waves that form as air near the wing approaches the speed of sound.
s1091: At cruise, air over the wing can locally go faster than sound and form a shock wave, sometimes visible as a shimmering line on the wing.
s1093: Altimeters measure air pressure, not height above the ground. High up, every pilot sets the same standard pressure, 1013.25 hPa, so planes stay safely apart.
s1095: Near the ground, a radio altimeter bounces signals off the surface to measure the exact height — that’s the voice calling “fifty, forty, thirty…” at landing.
s1097: Pilots read coded weather reports called METARs. “VHHH 221200Z 09012KT” means Hong Kong airport, 12:00 UTC on the 22nd, wind from 090° at 12 knots.
s1098: Planes that talk to each other
s1099: TCAS lets nearby planes’ computers talk; if two get too close, one is told to climb and the other to descend.
s1101: Many planes broadcast their position by ADS-B about once a second — that’s how flight-tracking apps can show planes live on a map.
s1103: Inertial systems use ring laser gyroscopes: laser beams travel both ways around a loop, and tiny differences reveal the plane’s rotation.
s1105: Great-circle routes look curved on a flat map, but on a globe they are the straightest possible path between two places.
s1107: The common Mercator map makes Greenland look about as big as Africa, but Africa is roughly 14 times larger.
s1109: Jet streams form where cold polar air meets warmer air. The temperature difference plus Earth’s spin can drive winds faster than 300 km/h.
s1111: The top of the troposphere is higher over the equator (about 17 km) than near the poles (about 8 km).
s1113: Air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 metres you climb — one reason mountain tops are snowy.
s1115: The speed of sound depends on temperature, not pressure. It is slower in cold air, so Mach 0.85 means fewer km/h at cruising height than at sea level.
s1117: Instruments show indicated airspeed from air pressure, but in thin air the true speed is much higher — at cruise, often nearly twice the indicated speed.
s1119: Ground speed is true airspeed plus or minus the wind. With a 150 km/h tailwind, a plane cruising at 900 km/h covers ground at 1,050 km/h.
s1121: Airline computers use a cost index to pick a cruising speed that balances the price of fuel against the cost of time.
s1123: Flight plans carry extra fuel to divert to another airport, plus a final reserve of about 30 minutes’ flying.
s1125: Each Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engine on an A350-1000 produces about 97,000 pounds (430 kN) of thrust.
s1127: Jet engines push huge amounts of air backwards, so the plane is pushed forwards — Newton’s third law in action.
s1129: A jet engine does four jobs in a row: intake (suck), compression (squeeze), combustion (bang) and exhaust (blow).
s1131: Carbon fibre conducts electricity less well than aluminium, so composite planes have a fine copper mesh in their skin to carry lightning safely.
s1133: Every flight inflates the fuselage like a balloon and lets it down again. New planes are tested through many thousands of these cycles.
s1135: Early Comet jets suffered from metal fatigue around square-cornered openings — one reason plane windows have rounded corners today.
s1136: A runway built on the sea
s1137: Hong Kong’s Three-Runway System added a 3,800-metre runway on about 650 hectares of land reclaimed from the sea.
s1139: Hong Kong doesn’t use daylight saving time but London does, so the time difference is 8 hours in winter and 7 hours in summer.
s1141: The International Date Line zigzags around island nations so that each country keeps a single date.
s1143: Earth bulges at the equator: its diameter there is about 43 km more than from pole to pole.
s1145: GPS satellite clocks run fast compared with clocks on Earth because of relativity. The system corrects for about 38 microseconds a day.
s1147: GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km up. A receiver needs signals from at least four to work out its position and the exact time.
s1148: Short flights burn more per km
s1149: Take-off and climb use a lot of fuel, so very short flights burn more fuel per kilometre than medium-length ones.
s1151: Today sustainable aviation fuel is blended with regular jet fuel; approved standards currently allow blends of up to 50%.
s1153: Contrails form when hot, moist exhaust meets air colder than about −40 °C. They only linger when that air is already very humid.
s1155: A ring around the Sun or Moon, called a 22° halo, is light bending through six-sided ice crystals in high cirrus clouds.
s1157: On polar routes at night you might see the aurora, made when particles from the Sun hit gases high in our atmosphere.
s1159: Flying high means slightly more cosmic radiation because there is less air above to shield you. For passengers, one flight’s dose is very small.
s1161: A popular explanation says air over the top of a wing must meet the air underneath at the back. It’s a myth — air over the top actually arrives first.
s0676: The secret is in the shape of the wings.
s0677: Airplane wings are curved on top and flatter on the bottom. As air moves over the wing, it creates a force called lift that pushes the plane upward. Combined with engine thrust pushing the plane forward, lift is what keeps a 200-tonne jet in the sky!
s0679: Meet the aircraft flying you today.
s0680: The Airbus A350-1000 can carry over 350 passengers and fly more than 8,000 miles without stopping. Its wings are partly made of carbon fibre, making it lighter and more fuel efficient than older jets.
s0683: Learn to spot cumulus, cirrus and stratus clouds.
s0684: Cumulus clouds look like fluffy cotton balls and usually mean fair weather. Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, found high in the sky. Stratus clouds form flat, grey layers that can bring drizzle.
s0685: Why Do Ears Pop on a Plane?
s0688: As a plane climbs, air pressure outside drops. Your middle ear has trapped air that needs to equalize, which is why swallowing, yawning, or chewing gum can help your ears feel better.
s0691: Many countries design unique passport stamps featuring local landmarks, animals, or symbols. Collecting stamps is like building a scrapbook of your adventures across the globe.
s0694: What does it take to fly for a living?
s0695: Pilots train for years, learning navigation, weather patterns, and how to handle emergencies. They work closely with air traffic control and their co-pilot to get everyone safely to their destination.
